newsitem.title: UK: Thatcher says will fight for Conservative victory.
newsitem.headline: Thatcher says will fight for Conservative victory.

text.p: Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher on Monday emphatically endorsed her successor, John Major, and dismissed media reports she was impressed by opposition leader Tony Blair.
Pledging to fight all out for a Conservative victory in Britain's May 1 election, she said Labour would raise taxes in government.
"Stay with us and with John Major until we cross the finishing line," Thatcher, ousted by her party in 1990, told reporters outside her London office.
Thatcher's relations with Major have often been stormy since he replaced her in 10, Downing Street.

She has sniped at his handling of Britain's links with Europe, the issue that finally brought her down, and damned him with faint praise in her autobiography, saying he lacked the courage to seize big ideas and just "drifted with the tide".

Last week Thatcher, still revered by right-wing Conservatives, was said by the left-wing Tribune newspaper to have told the editor of The Times at a private gathering that if Blair won power, "he won't let Britain down".
Thatcher's office said it did not know where the report had come, although it stopped short of an outright denial.
But after Major finally announced the election date on Monday, Thatcher swung behind the party which has held office since she led it to victory in 1979.
"The phrase New Labour is cunningly designed to conceal a lot of old socialism," she said.
"I have heard people say time for a change'. That's absurd. If you have a good builder, dare I say it, a good grocer, or a good government, you don't change, you stick with them."

Thatcher, the daughter of a grocer, also attacked Labour's claim that it would stay within the government's current spending targets, saying a Labour government always spent more money than a Conservative one.
Her statement included no reference to the reports of her conversation with the editor of the Times.
But in reply to reporters' questions, Thatcher said her endorsement of Major left no room for misunderstanding. "I do not expect to see Prime Minister Blair," she said.

"I'm fighting for Prime Minister Major and I'm fighting on with every effort I can," said Thatcher. She said she had already received more than 50 requests to speak at campaign meetings and more invitations were flooding in.
Despite Thatcher's endorsement, Major faces a herculean task in the election. Polls put Labour 25 points or so ahead, a margin no British government has overcome in the time available.
